common_name: Fireworks Rex Begonia (Radiating Metallic-Silver Spiral Foliage)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Fireworks performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F. Rex begonias prefer high humidity and consistent, moderate soil moisture without wet foliage.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Fireworks is a striking Rex begonia cultivar whose leaves radiate bands of metallic silver from a dark burgundy-black center out toward the leaf margin, creating a starburst pattern that gives the variety its name and catches light dramatically in a shaded room or patio. Like other Rex begonias it is grown entirely for its extraordinary foliage rather than its small, secondary flowers, which are often pinched off to keep energy directed into leaf production. Water at the soil level only to avoid leaf spot and powdery mildew, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and divide or take leaf cuttings to propagate and refresh an aging clump.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rex Begonia Variety Classification
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rex Begonias for Florida Interiors and Shade Gardens

common_name: Sparks Will Fly Rex Begonia (Deep Burgundy Silver-Spiral Foliage)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Sparks Will Fly performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Sparks Will Fly is a Rex begonia cultivar with deep burgundy-purple leaves overlaid by a bright metallic-silver spiral band that swirls in toward the leaf center, giving each leaf strong contrast and a shimmering quality in indirect light. As with other Rex begonias, the foliage is the entire point of growing it, and the small pink flowers that occasionally appear are typically removed to keep the plant's energy in leaf production. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot and powdery mildew, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and take leaf or stem cuttings to propagate new plants and rejuvenate an older, leggy clump.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rex Begonia Variety Classification
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Rex Begonias for Florida Interiors and Shade Gardens

planting.note: Plant transplants or hanging baskets after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to partial shade March-May. Bonfire blooms most heavily with some morning sun but wants afternoon shade in Gulf South heat.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in partial shade with some morning sun, in a hanging basket or container where the cascading stems can spill over the edge. Bonfire is a Begonia boliviensis hybrid grown for its long, arching, fuchsia-like stems smothered from early summer through frost in brilliant, narrow, flame-orange-red tubular flowers, giving a nonstop, blazing display far heavier than most traditional tuberous begonias. Unlike large-flowered tuberous begonias, it shrugs off heat and rain without the flowers turning to mush, making it a much more reliable performer through humid Gulf South summers. Deadheading is unnecessary since it is self-cleaning, but pinching stem tips early in the season encourages fuller, bushier growth. Where winters bring hard freezes, bring the tuber or a rooted cutting indoors before frost to overwinter, since the plant is not reliably hardy outside zone 9 and warmer.

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May. Benitochiba performs well as an outdoor container plant in summer and an indoor houseplant when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil, and stake or support the upright cane-like stems as the plant matures. Benitochiba is a cane-type (angel-wing) begonia with large, asymmetrical, olive-bronze leaves heavily dotted in silvery-white spots and washed with red on the undersides, giving it a bold, jungle-like presence that holds up well as an accent plant even without its clusters of pink flowers. It grows taller and more upright than Rex or rhizomatous begonias, forming a multi-stemmed shrubby clump over a season or two, and benefits from occasional pinching of cane tips to encourage bushier branching. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and bring potted plants indoors before frost where winters are not reliably frost-free.

common_name: Home Run Rose (Disease-Resistant Red Landscape Rose)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun (at least 6 hours direct sun) for best bloom production and disease resistance.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Home Run was bred by Bailey Nurseries as an improvement on the original Knock Out rose, sharing its extreme disease resistance and continuous rebloom but adding true immunity to black spot rather than just strong resistance, along with a slightly more compact, rounded habit that fits smaller landscape spaces. The single, bright cherry-red flowers with a small white eye at the base bloom in repeated flushes from spring through fall, and the plant is self-cleaning, so spent blooms drop cleanly without deadheading. Like Knock Out, Home Run needs no fungicide spraying in most climates to stay healthy through humid Gulf South summers. Prune back hard in late winter, cutting the whole plant to 12-18 inches, to stimulate vigorous new growth and the heaviest bloom for the coming season.
sources: Bailey Nurseries — Home Run Rose Introduction
